task_brief: This is day 6 of "Patterns, Sequences, and Introductory Algorithms". That is unit 4 in grade 3. Today is a correction and reflection about simple repeat patterns. It takes about 40–60 minutes. It is one day's work, not the whole unit project. Your unit is working toward this: Write and test a step-by-step set of directions for a partner or character to follow. Today helps by working on simple repeat patterns. Your unit also covers what is an algorithm, everyday sequences, giving step-by-step directions, and following a partner's directions. Today adds real evidence toward your unit project.
primary_task: Look back at your earlier work on simple repeat patterns and fix it. Make a fix-it list. For each mistake write four things: what went wrong, why it went wrong, what you changed, and how you know it works now. Include one thing that failed before and works now. Then look at all your mistakes together. What do they have in common? Name one habit that would catch it sooner. Everything you need is printed in activity_setup. It has the exact case, what should happen, how to try it, checks, and a paper choice worth the same score. Do not wait for another handout or app. Keep today's work tied to your unit. Today is about simple repeat patterns. It is part of "Patterns, Sequences, and Introductory Algorithms". Later days in this unit cover other things, like what is an algorithm. Before you stop, do this check: In one concise response, show or explain the most important idea about simple repeat patterns; then identify one check that would catch an error or weak claim. In grade 3 you need one clear try with a grown-up nearby. Say or write your reason in a sentence or two. Drawings, objects, or spoken answers are all fine.

central_input.purpose: Design only for the fictional learner described here; no interview, public post, account, camera, or outside tester is needed.
central_input.fictional_user: Kai uses a keyboard, sometimes enlarges text to 200%, and wants a three-step way to track completed reading sessions without entering a name or location.

Show completion using both a word and a visual mark, not color alone.

expected_behavior_and_specification: The response must apply simple repeat patterns to at least three labelled details from the supplied central input.
Every conclusion must identify the exact row, card, requirement, or scenario sentence that supports it.
The response must include one concrete revision or decision and explain the check that would show whether it worked.
The response must name one thing the supplied case does not tell you instead of guessing.

execution_method.primary: Paper-first method: copy the short labels, annotate them, and complete the response in a notebook or any notes app. No download, installation, account, or internet access is needed.
execution_method.local_optional: A locally available word processor, spreadsheet, drawing tool, or slide editor may be used, but no particular brand or paid feature is required.
execution_method.check_path: Use the numbered specification and the package test/check criteria as a checklist; a parent or tutor can verify the cited labels without needing subject software.

debugging_target.passing_change: A reader can trace every conclusion to a printed label in the central input and can perform the stated check without outside materials.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: Everything in this task runs in a sandbox or on paper. Never use a real password, passphrase, API key, account credential, access token, precise home location, or any real person's identifiable information — invent fictional values instead. Do not sign into, probe, scan, stress, or attempt access to any live, production, school, or third-party system, and do not bypass a filter, licence, access control, or terms of service. Any practice login used in an example must be obviously invented — a silly made-up name paired with a nonsense multi-word phrase — and must never be anything you or anyone in your family actually uses somewhere real. If a task seems to need something real, substitute a made-up stand-in and note the substitution.

copyright_and_authorship: The graded submission must be your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI tool may explain an idea, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but must not produce, write, debug, or make any part of the work that is scored. Any code, asset, or text you did not write must be openly licensed or supplied for this task, and must be cited in a comment or note naming where it came from and what you changed.

Preserve the learning target while adjusting quantity, pacing, representation, or response mode.
task_accessibility_provisions: You can do this with the keyboard only, no mouse needed. Text can be made bigger, and you may do it on paper instead of a screen.
You can take a break, stretch, or come back to this later. That does not lower your score.
safety_and_privacy_rules: Allow a pause, break, or alternate response mode without treating it as failure.
Never require a real password, private message, precise location, account credential, API key, or identifiable image.
Use only fictional or sandboxed systems, accounts, and data; never probe, exploit, or attempt to access a real external system.
Use approved sites and tools; do not bypass filters, access controls, licensing, or terms of service.

media.suggestion: Optional diagram, map, worked example, source image, demonstration, or short clip supporting simple repeat patterns.
media.fallback: Provide the same information as readable steps, alt text, transcript, tactile/concrete model, or teacher demonstration.

remediation: Reteaching for simple repeat patterns follows the signal actually observed, not a fixed script. If the signal is "prerequisite gap": Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for simple repeat patterns, model it with a concrete or text-only representation, then retry one fresh item. If the signal is "procedure without understanding": Ask the learner to explain or represent why the process for simple repeat patterns works before continuing. If the signal is "correct but low confidence": Confirm the reasoning specifically, offer one varied example of simple repeat patterns, and avoid unnecessary remediation. If the signal is "repeated error pattern": Name the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a worked example, and schedule a short same-day or next-session review. If the signal is "mastery evidence": Require accurate independent application plus explanation on a later or different occasion before marking simple repeat patterns mastered. Re-check with one fresh item of the same kind before moving on, and record which signal was seen so the pattern is visible across the unit rather than treated as a one-off.
extension: Apply simple repeat patterns under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or teach the idea with an original example without completing another learner’s graded work. Treat this as optional depth on simple repeat patterns rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays inside the same sandbox rules — no real credentials and no live external systems. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.
